Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Do you speak Telugu?
Answer: I don't really speak Telugu at the moment (except for a few broken sentences), but I'm trying my best in learning the language so that I can speak fluently. That said, I do listen to people speaking Telugu and can make out the typical 'urban' coversation mixed with English words. I have quite a few Telugu friends: some - natives of Andhra Pradesh/ Telangana/ Yanam (one of the four enclaves of the Union Territory of Pondicherry) and few Telugus who have settled for good here in Pondicherry (my native place). They are my main source of learning Telugu. Them being the kind people they are, patiently teach me the essential basics, correct my sentences, grammar and pronunciation. Secondly, I get to watch Telugu movies in theatre (Telugu movies have a reasonable demand in Pondicherry since there is a sizeable Telugu speaking population based in Pondicherry itself and also students from the above said places), the most recent ones I watched being Rangasthalam and Geetha Govindam. Talking about the reading and writing part, I would say I'm better at reading and to some extent writing Telugu than speaking, thanks to my Kannada lineage. I can read, write (which have helped me in reading Telugu - explained later) and fluently speak Kannada. Kannada and Telugu scripts are close to each other (very few letters and the accents are different) and if somebody knows one, mastering the other doesn't take more than week or month if rigorously attempted. This is my humble try at writing Telugu ( I meant to write 'My name is Balakrishnan. I live in Pondicherry. Hope you are fine.' Blame Google translate if the translation is funny or wrong :P :D) Last, but not the least, Telugu songs are close to my heart. Be it the Carnatic music kritis/ varnas (I play the violin and these were my first lessons!) or contemporary Telugu music, they are there on my playlists! A long drive is never complete without listening to atleast a couple of Telugu songs. In fact there are certain remade / dubbed (from Tamil) Telugu movies whose songs I'm more confident with the lyrics and also singing (credit to repeat mode on mobile phone and promotion of these albums in the social media) than the original Tamil versions! Best examples I would cite include songs from the movies 'Kaala' (no offense Tamilians…but 'Chittemma' , I feel, is way better than 'Kannamma'), 'Ye Maaya Chesave' etc. So folks, that's the story of me and Telugu. Looking forward to learn more. Hopefully my next answer about Telugu would have few Telugu sentences!!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: How many Dravidian languages other than Kannada have native words (not those borrowed from Sanskrit) which starts with the letter 'ha'?
Answer: Thanks for A2A Goutham R (ಗೌತಮ್ ಆರ್) As a Tamil speaker, I can say there is no word in Tamil that starts with ‘ha’. The Tamil Alphabet has 247 letters and it doesn’t include ‘ha’. In fact, the letter ‘ஹ’ was developed/ introduced just for transliteration purposes. So when there is no such letter, there can be no words either! Also, the above said use is often condemned and words beginning with ‘ha’ are often Tamilized! —Mostly in cases of proper nouns (Names). E.g.) Hindu - இந்து (Indu), Haran - அரன் (Aran), Hosur - ஓசூர் (Osur) Moreover, Tamil has its own equivalents to all the Sanskrit words and the influence of Sanskrit even sans ‘ha’ is very less.

Question: What is the most unforgettable experience you had while grocery shopping?
Answer: I wouldn’t say unforgettable, but it is definitely a fond memory! August 2016 I had just come back to Pondicherry, my hometown, after a month’s vacation at dad’s in Tanzania. Even if Complan’s claims were true, it wouldn’t apply for me. I was already 19 years old, with completed growth spurt and a height of 172 cm. But when your teacher jokes around, logic doesn’t matter! I did stop drinking Complan few months later and switched over to coffee! (Picture from Google Images)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What are the correct words for lockdown in Hindi and Tamil?
Answer: I’ll restrict my answer to only Tamil as my proficiency in Hindi is, well, no comments! Tamil is probably the only South Indian language that has minimal Sanskrit influence. Even if the existing Sanskrit words are removed, there are plenty of equivalent native words. What is more interesting is, substituting such Sanskrit or English words with native Tamil words doesn’t make the language sound odd after all! The word ‘lockdown’ is no exception; ‘ஊரடங்கு’ (Ooradangu) or ‘பொதுமுடக்கம்’ (Podhumudakkam), which are the Tamil equivalents for ‘lockdown’ are amongst the most frequently heard words in media of late! This doesn’t seem to be the case with many other regional media news channels I’ve watched. They simply use the word ‘lockdown’ Multiple other words related to COVID are also rendered in Tamil by the media. The people welcome such usage of Tamil words with warmth and pride. Attaching below two images of news regarding the same matter (black fungus cases), but in different languages. It is evident how Tamil media sticks to native words (black fungus = கருப்பு பூஞ்சை (karuppu poonjai)) while other regional media simply refer to the same in English! (Image source: ‘Hindu - Tamil Thisai’ newspaper app) (Image source: ‘Vijaya Karnataka’ newspaper app)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is the most badass thing your parent has ever done?
Answer: Early 2000s… Maybe 2003 or 2004. Back then, I do not think high speed broadband Internet connections existed, at least at our hometown Pondicherry. We had this age old BSNL dial-up Internet connection, connected to the landline telephone. It required us to log in with a password every time we needed to access the internet. Also, while using internet, if one was to pick up a call on the landline, internet connection would get disconnected and the log-in procedure had to be repeated. We had an internet connection at home mainly because dad had to check E-mails when not at work and clear them off before the next day. Needless to say, it was not an era of smartphones. The very concept of internet was fascinating for my sister and me! We felt thrilled being able to get information about anything with just few clicks, browse different websites and communicate through E-mails with family contacts living as far as in the USA. Contrary to Google, Yahoo’s home page itself would be awesome with multiple featured news items, links directing to Mail, Answers, Messenger, Stock market, Weather and what not! I guess it still is like that, although the traffic on the site is multifold less than Google. But what caught our eyes every time was ‘GAMES’! Yahoo used to have this concept of ‘Downloadable Games’. Only the trial version of these games could be downloaded. Full version required us to pay online in US Dollars, which was unimaginable for us. The trial version included 60 minutes of free game play, after the expiry of which only 5 minutes of gameplay would be allowed every time the game was opened. We were permitted to download only one such game every week or every 10 days, as the internet bills were also relatively expensive those days. We were allowed to access the internet only when our father was at home. We didn’t have a choice either, because only he knew the password. This was mainly to prevent us from downloading multiple games and escalating the internet bills, and of course the keep a check of our activity in the internet. Our dad was and is still a workaholic. Even when he was at home, he used to be occupied with office work. We had to ask him to log-in for us whenever we had to download games from the internet or every time the internet connection got disconnected because mom picked up a random landline call🙆🏻‍♂️. This was very frustrating for us, as kids! We promised him we would not exceed the download limit and not use the computer when he was not home, and requested for the password. He did not budge. The password was a mystery known only to him for few more years, until one day we both sneaked in close to him and saw him typing it! My sister and I never felt more fooled or dumber till date in our lives! The password was no complex alpha-numerical word or phrase, but ‘studioworks’, after all! Studioworks was the name of that particular model of LG monitor, boldly printed over it, right in front of our eyes! *Facepalm🙆🏻‍♂️🙈* This, by far, is the most badass thing my parent(dad) has ever done! (Picture from Google Image search)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: As an Indian, what's your favourite thing about India?
Answer: Food! I’m a strong believer of ‘Be a Roman when in Rome’. While travelling or moving out of India to another country, adapting to changes might prove to be a difficult task. But, in the long run, that is what will help one express themself and interact better, with the local population. Be it language, lifestyle or culture, adapting to the new place offers its own advantages! This can also be applied to regional differences within India. But, one exception is FOOD! Nothing beats Indian food. No wonder millions of Non-Resident Indians/ Persons of Indian Origin prefer and have Indian food, regardless of how long they’ve been away from home. No amount of westernisation has killed the charm and heritage of Indian cuisines. (Pictures from Google Images) It’s not that I always have Indian food wherever I go. I do explore new places, new restaurants and cuisines abroad; all of that probably for a maximum of couple of days. The Indian in me would then crave for the authentic, spicy, aromatic Indian food! Finding an Indian restaurant in an unknown land is like a child lost in a carnival, finally finding its parents! Though I’m a South Indian, I like South Indian and North Indian cuisines alike. Being in a different country is when, we realize, being an Indian is more important than finding differences within us based on region, language etc. @ Khana Khazana Indian restaurant, Kigali (Rwanda) Now, Rwanda is an East-African country where there isn’t even a reasonable expatriate Indian population. So what?! Demand initiates supply, and I could see so many Rwandans themselves having Indian food there. That said, how can I not love Indian food, as an Indian myself?! <3

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is your salary? Are you happy with it?
Answer: I’m a doctor and I’m paid ₹5,000 per month. Obviously, I’m not happy with it. I’m currently a Compulsory Rotatory Residential Intern (CRRI) doctor/ House Surgeon at the Government Medical College - Hospital of Pondicherry. We started our internship on February 19th, 2020. A month later, COVID-19 was in the news and soon our hospital became the state’s COVID designated hospital and all other services were shut. Today, with 13500+ total cases and 211 deaths, Pondicherry tops the country in the number of positive COVID-19 cases per million! Ever since there were interns in our hospital (from 2015), this amount of ₹5000 has been the standard monthly stipend. No payslip, no Government Order, no whatsoever. It comes to ₹161/ day which is far less than most daily wage labourers in the country. Even worse, the stipend is not credited to our bank accounts every month. It is usually credited at the end of three months as ₹15,000. This stipend amount is the least of all Government Medical Colleges in the country. Funny fact is that ours is allegedly the country’s most expensive Government Medical College, tuition-fee wise. It used to be ₹70,000/year when I was a UG student. Now, I understand it is 1 lakh+ per year, from my juniors. Multiple attempts in representing this issue to the government, including indefinite student strikes, RTI complaints etc. yielded nothing. Whilst this stipend amount is not acceptable even during normal times, imagine working day and night during a pandemic period for ₹161/ day. Our valuable training period is also lost in the name of COVID-19. We have completely lost hope on the government regarding stipend hike. Therefore, we have not resorted to any more strikes. We have been posted in all areas of the COVID hospital including COVID wards, COVID ICU and casualty. While this unhappy and unrewarded feeling will definitely continue to prevail, I’m sure this has, not in anyway, affected the healthcare we provide to our patients, nor will it in the future. This holds good, COVID or not :) (Picture from my phone gallery)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Is it necessary to clean shave in medical college?
Answer: Not necessarily. Whilst most medical colleges do have a dress code, there’s no written rule that boys will have to clean shave. However, many professors (Females >>> Males) believe that a ‘clean shaven face’ is an integral part of professionalism, and frown on beards. They enforce it during their lectures, practical classes and clinical postings. Most of us, especially during the early years of MBBS, religiously follow their instructions. With passing time, adherence to the same decreases :D One of our microbiology professors was fond of picking on boys with the slightest growth of beard (Moustache was allowed as most Tamilians are not comfortable shaving off their moustache). I had only then (2016) developed a liking for the French beard and tried to sport one. He promptly called me to his desk and the conversation went as follows: Sir: Why have you not shaved your beard? And…what is this style? Me: Sir, I… just… Sir: Are you sporting this beard because you like it, or because… someone special asked you to? Me: Sir, sir… nothing like that! Sir: Because, if that’s the case, I won’t ask you to clean shave! Otherwise, you’ll have to. Me: I’ll shave off, sir :P But, I never shaved! After second year MBBS, nobody really asked us to trim/ shave unless the overall appearance was rugged with unironed clothes/ unkempt hair etc. We just had to maintain a decent dress code, especially while attending the clinical postings. In fact, one of the surgeons openly said having beard was OK, provided we maintained it properly. He himself tried and sported different beard styles regularly! An interesting scenario: Final practical exams! A popular saying in the medico community of India goes like ‘MBBS degree is not taken, it is given!’. One never knows which (external) examiner has what opinions about looks. Few of them still have opinions like ‘First impression is the best impression’, ‘Face is the index of the mind’ etc. and judge the student based on whether they have shaved/ not; wear clean, ironed aprons/ not; wear polished shoes/ not and what not! Few of them are much more open-minded and evaluate the student(s) only for their clinical competence. Naturally, medical students leave no stone unturned to pass these final exams! Because it is difficult to predict which of the above two categories the examiner would belong to, none of us took a chance during our final practical examinations. It is that season of the year, where you would spot clean shaved faces everywhere in the campus! Even the ‘big macho tough guy’ would look like a child :D (Me on the day of last practical exam of first year MBBS!)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Can Indians and Pakistanis be friends?
Answer: If somebody’s nationality is the sole criterion that stops you from making or being friends with them, then it would never qualify as friendship in the first place; you would also need to introspect your thought process in that case! At the same time, I do not opine all friendships are meant to stay. We have all had best friends who became strangers later. Was it because the friend was a different national? Well, not really! Whether two people can be friends depends on a lot more factors than just nationality, in fact nationality should never be a factor that makes or breaks a friendship. I have friends from every country that I got a chance to visit. If this question comes from a religious context, the answer is of course ‘Yes, Indians and Pakistanis can be friends!’ Few friendships also have the privilege of transforming into love stories that culminate into marriages! Do we have such Indian-Pakistani love stories? Hell, yeah! If this question is from a political context, the answer is still ‘Yes, Indians and Pakistanis can be friends!’ If the question is from a linguistic context, the answer is still ‘Yes, Indians and Pakistanis can be friends!’ I guess the whole ‘India vs. Pakistan’ idea is a very local one restricted only to these two countries. Once I am out of India, or a Pakistani friend is out of Pakistan in a foreign land, we’re both recognised as Asians! In Africa, I’ve been asked if I’m a Bangladeshi or a Pakistani or an Indian, looking at my skin tone. They don’t even know unless we tell them; we’re just Asians to them. Pakistan, or India, doesn’t matter to them as long as they get business. Similarly, Indians and Pakistanis share workplaces, businesses and friendships in several parts of the world, especially in the Gulf and the UK. When such smooth dealings are possible outside our native lands, why not here? While I was on a street tour in Dubai, the cab driver was kind enough to go out of his way and show me every possible place that could be covered within half a day. He would have definitely figured out that I was from India; he was still friendly, he was still doing his job with utmost dedication! Guess what? He was a Pakistani! And there’s this Pakistani gentleman whom every medical student on Earth admires and reveres. He’s a role model to thousands of budding doctors and is undoubtedly one of the greatest medical teachers the world has ever seen - Dr. Najeeb! Do you think any sane Indian would not want to be friends with him, just because he’s a Pakistani?!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What was the oddest question you were ever asked by airport security?
Answer: May, 2011 Back then, my dad was working for a Container Glass Industry in Nigeria. We (Mom and I) had gone to visit him during the summer break. Almost a month later, it was time for us to return home. Place: Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, Nigeria. There were two Emirates flights to Dubai (our connecting airport en route Chennai) per day, one that departed in the afternoon, reaching Dubai in the night. The other one, departing at around 09:30 pm and reaching Dubai early morning next day. We were booked in the latter. Now, this route (Lagos - Dubai) is a very busy and fully-booked one, considering the worldwide air connections available from Dubai and also the trade in Nigeria. This reflected on our flight too. There were very long queues for boarding! Felt like it would take ages for economy class passengers to be called. (Emirates has an ‘all wide-body’ aircraft fleet and hence boarding is always a Himalayan task). The scene was exactly like below So, we were waiting, worn out and apathetic. Suddenly, an announcement was made: “Passengers travelling with infants and kids are now invited to board the aircraft”. OK! So when this happened, I was 14 years old, a 10th grader at school! I wasn’t an infant (obviously ;) ) NOR A ‘KID’! Therefore, neither mom nor I reacted to the announcement. Cutting the crowd, a lady from the security came, straight towards us! And she directly talks to my mom (with a strong African accent), “Madam, why are you standing here? We just called passengers travelling with kids!” I retaliated reflexly, “I’M NOT A KID”. She was too cool to get offended. She asked a simple question and gave an all new definition to the term ‘kid’! “Are you married?!” So, that was the oddest question that I was ever asked in an airport, considering the fact that I was a 14-year old adolescent male! LOL. P.S: I replied “No”, and she confirmed my ‘kid’ status and made us board with other ‘kid’ families! (Pictures taken from Google images)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is most important in learning English?
Answer: I feel mastering the grammar is more important than any other aspect in learning English, or any other language for that matter. Pronunciation of many words varies widely from region to region; there is no single accepted or rather ‘correct’ pronunciation. However, standard pronunciation can be developed by watching international news channels, listening to online radio stations or watching English movies (does not really serve the purpose, considering the usage of slang words and colloquialism) Vocabulary, on the other hand, is quite challenging. Building one’s vocabulary is a lifetime process. So, it can be taken slowly. Learning a certain number of new words (say, five) and constructing sentences using those words would really help a novice. Even otherwise, good company like native speakers or co-learners will prove to be of great help in improving and improvising the vocabulary. Therefore, I feel, Grammar is the most important. Because, building a strong vocabulary and developing ‘perfect pronunciation’, still with grammatical mistakes, is a big turn-off! A person with poor grammar is always looked down upon, at least in a professional set-up!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If Tamil Nadu is exempted from NEET, can the whole of India ask for an exemption from the NEET?
Answer: I am not sure of the legal probabilities with respect to this question. But the method of admitting students into MBBS has to be a state decision. If admission through Board Exam score is what they want, give them that! I cleared my higher secondary exams in March 2014. I am from Pondicherry and we follow(ed) the Tamil Nadu State Board syllabus. I can vouch for it. It was of high standard and exhaustive. Recent TN textbooks are even more exhaustive and wholesome, preparing the student for NEET-PG exams. Question: Then why is it opposed? Why should the students of TN/ PY not give NEET-PG? Answer: Why should they give?! I was admitted into the Government Medical College of my state based on my board exam marks. What mishap happened? I can safely tell I’m doing fine. I can reasonably approach and confidently treat all illnesses and diseases an MBBS graduate is expected to treat; I can give public health education at village and community level; I can provide basic wound care that includes suturing and dressing; etc. On the contrary, clearing a so-called competitive exam and entering a medical college gives no assurance that the student would automatically become one of the best doctors of the country. It is the dedication and commitment one has during the course of his or her MBBS which decides the kind of professional they become in future. Moreover, hundreds of my seniors from Pondicherry and Tamil Nadu, who were admitted into MBBS based on Higher Secondary Board Exam marks, are in very prestigious institutions like AIIMS-New Delhi, PGI-Chandigarh, NIMHANS-Bengaluru, etc. doing their residency now. Where comes quality of medical professionals here? There are thousands of successful, contemporary doctors from TN and PY who got into MBBS (until 2016) using their board exam marks. Chennai is still one of the leading cities in the world for Medical tourism! So, what is in an entrance exam?! After all, admission through board exam marks was also by a carefully designed counselling system. ‘Biology-Physics-Chemistry (BPC) cut-offs’ used to be as high as 199.9 for General Category students and many a time not less than 197, even for reserved categories! Scoring that high in board exams is not a child’s play! Only the best of the best hard workers could achieve that feat. Now why introduce another tough exam for entry into MBBS? Isn’t it like an insult to their year-long hardwork and efforts to fare well in the Higher Secondary exam? If board exam marks don’t guarantee qualified doctors in the future and only an exam like NEET can do the job, then why have schools and board exams?! Those kids who intend to become doctors should be able to straightaway enrol themselves in coaching classes, right?! But that’s not the system in place! The only instance where I advocate entrance exam for admission to MBBS is for filling up of the All India Quota (AIQ) seats in state medical colleges. Each state follows a different syllabus. It would be illogical to come up with a ranklist of students with different state syllabi for MBBS admission into the AIQ seats available in the medical colleges throughout India. (Do NOT immediately suggest unification of syllabus throughout India! Anything that has zero diversity is detrimental for a country as big as India!) Therefore, each state should ideally have its own MBBS admission strategy for the 85% state quota seats. This may be through the Higher Secondary Board exam marks or through a common entrance test for the state candidates alone. This decision has to be based on the interest of the majority; in this case - concerned students, teachers and parents. In addition, candidates of all states must have the option to sit for the All India level common entrance exam (AIPMT/ NEET) which would be the single entrance exam for filling up of the 15% AIQ seats across Indian medical colleges. வாழு, வாழ விடு! (Live and let live!)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is everyone doing during the coronavirus?
Answer: As such, my routine remains undisturbed. Coronavirus has probably made me more cautious and self-protective at workplace. I have been working as an intern/ House surgeon at the Government Hospital of my town. I have completed two postings viz Ophthalmology and Otolaryngology. Currently, I’m posted in the department of Dermatology. Over the last few weeks, I have keenly been following the news and the rate at which Coronavirus is on the rise. From 28 cases 15 days ago, to 165+ cases and 5 deaths today, the magnitude of the disease is scary. We have always followed universal precautions at workplace like frequent hand washing, using hand rubs after attending to every patient and wearing masks where required. I would say, the emphasis and the frequency of these activities have increased. From sweepers to the Heads of Departments, everybody is seen adorning masks; hand sanitizers are used like never before; anybody who coughs attracts extensive attention from by-standers; so on and so forth. We have strictly limited the number of outpatients that come to the hospital and very stringent rules have been laid out as to who and how many can accompany the patients. No elective surgeries are being done and non-COVID19 inpatients are being discharged. Adequate medications are being given and all patients are asked to review in NOT less than 4 weeks. On a personal note, I’ve started to avoid any type of social gathering. No hangouts with friends, not even that long walk in the beach. All of that can wait! I go to work because I have to. Had I not been a doctor, I would have happily remained home doing things I love. The service of doctors, be it for screening Corona suspects or tracking contacts or treating the affected at the earliest, is indispensable. Most other professionals can work from home. Remember, hospitals are melting pots of all kinds of infections and Corona is no exception given the current scenario. I kindly request people to refrain from going to hospitals for minor illnesses like body aches or refractive errors. It can only get you and your loved ones COVID-19. So, here I am, working at my hospital at the time of a major crisis.

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is the saddest moment you have seen in a movie or TV?
Answer: Background story: A father (widower) of four kids. He is bankrupt as he has recently been suspended from his job on charges of embezzlement. His only family members are: -Elder Son, who has despised his family and lives in the United States, so much so that he wouldn’t even come back to his mother’s funeral. -Younger son, who is a prodigal with no proper educational qualification and constantly at loggerheads with his family. -Elder daughter, married off to a typical, rich patriarchal Indian family, which is not supportive of her going to a job or visiting her dad or giving him money. -Younger daughter, who had a Poliomyelitis attack as a child and is physically challenged. -An extremely orthodox brother-in-law who deals with his own financial and family problems! This gentleman has turned to alcoholism for his solace, further worsening his poverty. At this juncture, he plans to get rid of his only burden, his younger daughter, by marrying her off to a prospective groom. But as fate would have it, nobody comes forward to marry the girl as she is physically challenged. Even otherwise, many reject her, as she is not from a well-to-do family! Finally a guy approaches her dad, asking her hand in marriage. Apparently, he’s not behind money or looks or anything, but he wants to marry her for who she is! Sounds wonderful, doesn’t it? But, the story isn’t that simple or merry! When the father brings up this proposal to his daughter, she comes to know that the prospective groom is 46 years old! He emotionally blackmails her that it was her mother’s last wish to get the girl married. He argues that her mother’s soul wouldn’t rest in peace, in case she refuses to marry the only guy who came forward to marry her. Having no choice as a helpless daughter to a drunk widower, the poor girl agrees to meet the boy. At this point, the dad is taken aback. He was expecting some retaliation from his daughter. But the fact that she instantly agreed to his proposal makes him feel guilty. In order to overcome it, he tells her, ‘It’s not a compulsion. I’m not telling that you must marry him. Just see him tomorrow; if you like him, well and good! Otherwise, all that we have to lose is a cup of coffee!’ The distraught daughter replies, ‘Don’t worry dad, I don’t think a 46-year-old(or young?!) groom would probably need sugar to his coffee!’ This is by far the saddest, and probably, the deepest scene I have ever seen on television! It captures the vulnerability of not just physically challenged, but also most poor girls in India. From the 1990s Kannada television series, Mayamruga aired on DD Chandana and later on Zee Kannada. (All pictures from YouTube, where the series is now available 😊)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is your favourite word in your native language?
Answer: I was born and (being) brought up in Pondicherry, India. So my native language is Tamil. There are a lot of favourite words that I can think of, Tamil being very ancient and one of the most beautiful langauges. But, I would like to share that one word which awed me at the very first sight! It is 'நோயீனிகடத்தி' (noyeenikadathi) which means 'vector' (Biology) A 'vector' is an agent, usually an insect, that carries a disease-causing-organism in it. It goes about spreading infectious diseases. The above Tamil equivalent, of course, is not an ancient word. But it has been aptly coined as medical science evolved. It conveys the very definition of a biological vector! [நோய் (noi) = disease, நோயீனி (noyeeni) = Pathogen/ disease causing agent, கடத்தி (kadathi) = transmitter] I first came across this word when we went on a visit to The 'Vector Control Research Centre' (VCRC), as a part of our field training when we were posted in the Department of Preventive and Social Medicine (PSM) a.k.a Community Medicine. Not only was I impressed by the commendable, high level research and training activites going on in this institute, but also I thoroughly enjoyed learning this new word which has now become my most favourite Tamil word!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If I take an MD in physiology after an MBBS, is it successful in a small town?
Answer: Does the small town have a medical college? Is that a government medical college? Is there a vacancy for Assistant Professor of Physiology post, that you can apply for?! If the answers to the above questions are a yes, then ‘Yes, you will be successful!’ Nevertheless, your MD (Physiology) degree will place you at a higher pedestal than any MBBS doctor. Moreover, unlike, say MD Microbiology (which is essentially everything about all microbes), physiology is very closely linked with the clinical specialities as it deals with the functioning of human body, after all! Any doctor with a sound knowledge of physiology will be a successful person at that. Like General Practice? The combination of the knowledge of functioning of human body and *the MD degree* will do the magic! With dedicated and committed patient care, minimal investment and word-of-mouth marketing by happy patients, your private practice will flourish. Most of the times, this earning exceeds that of a junior level faculty member in a government medical college. You’ll just need patience! Changed your mind to move to a city? The number of medical colleges is increasing every passing year; prospects of your earning a decently paying teaching job isn’t that difficult! My hometown Pondicherry alone has a whopping 8 medical colleges for a population of around 2.5 lakhs! Also, how about starting a YouTube channel, writing an MCQ book or joining a PG coaching platform as mentor/ faculty part time?! Best wishes!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is the most thought-provoking comment you accidentally overheard about language learning?
Answer: Not ‘overheard’! But read from multiple answers and personal experiences here on Quora. Contrary to the common notion that infants get confused when exposed to multiple languages, they actually tend to pick up all the languages they’re exposed to. Children with parents of different languages/ linguistic backgrounds tend to pick up both the languages when there is equal exposure. When a language is learnt right from infancy, the speaker tends to have native level fluency even though it might not be his/ her mother tongue. Early training is the key! This, according to me, is probably the most though-provoking aspect about language learning!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What shocked you today?
Answer: Post completion of my MBBS, I’ve been preparing for my MD entrance exams. Two exams got over recently. As I will not be able to get a branch of my choice based on these exams’ scores, I’m appearing for the INICET exam to be held on 14th November, 2021 and preparing for the same. I had given a mock entrance exam couple of days ago and was reviewing the answers this morning. So, today was basically like any other day… until I saw this! One of my professors, who also happens to be a Kannadiga, had posted this status on WhatsApp. I could not process it. I was blank. I replied to her, asking what happened, why a black and white picture with broken hearts?? She was quick to reply that he had suffered a ‘massive heart attack’ and passed away! Praying this to be a rumour (there are way too many death rumours of late), I immediately googled ‘Puneeth Rajkumar’. There were many news articles that showed he was ‘critical’ and being treated in the ICU of a popular corporate hospital in Bangalore. A YouTube search also yielded similar results, with rather scary portraits. I rushed to the living room, switched on the TV and saw all Kannada news channels covering this single news: Puneeth Rajkumar’s critical health condition. I was still hopeful because not one news channel reported he had passed away! (Puneeth Rajkumar receiving treatment in ICU) (Chief Minister (of Karnataka) in conversation with the Rajkumar family) Once again, I asked my professor what actually was happening. She told he was no more but it was not yet official. To support her claim, she also sent a forwarded audio wherein a doctor from the hospital where Puneeth sir was admitted tells he had passed away, inspite of all their resuscitative efforts. She also sent a forwarded picture where Puneeth sir’s lifeless covered body was lying in the hospital stretcher. (These became public moments later) I was beginning to feel numb and emotionally troubled furthermore. I called up one of my friends in Bangalore. As we were talking over the developments, the TV screen flashed the much dreaded, most unfortunate news, I or anyone who follows Sandalwood, could’ve imagined. (Actor Puneeth Rajkumar no more) Like any other Kannadiga or Sandalwood fan, I was dumbstruck. This news felt like it came out of nowhere. Not in our wildest dreams would any of us have imagined such an untimely death for Sandalwood’s power star. As time passed by, more and more information kept pouring. As if the news of his very death was not enough, there were more and more heart wrenching information like he was perfectly alright this morning; he had been to gym; he had tweeted wishing his elder brother’s latest movie success; he had danced on a stage during the promotional event of the same movie, just two days back; he had been an active part of a music director’s birthday celebration last night; he was the chief guest of a hospital’s inaugural ceremony three days back; and what not?! (Puneeth sir’s tweet dated 29th October at 7.33 AM!! Life is freaking unpredictable!) Hundreds of celebrities tweeting condolences, sharing stories on Instagram, WhatsApp statuses filled with Puneeth’s photos… One thing was universal and common about all these posts. All that people could say was, ‘I cannot believe this happened/ can’t process this/ this is not possible’ and the like. Because that’s how it was and still is! It’s almost 12 hours since the bad news was out and millions of us are still SHOCKED. (One of the thousands of tweets, from Telugu actor Mahesh Babu) Puneeth sir was known for his fitness, after all! When such a fit and healthy person himself succumbs to heart attack, it only raises serious questions on our own lifestyle and its potential dangers. This is a bit clichéd, but I’m not able to stop myself from thinking of this - even Puneeth sir himself would’nt have anticipated something like this, a death like this! He’s one person in the industry with zero controversies. As is commonly pointed out, nepotism is there in South Indian film industry too. But unlike other regions, nobody becomes successful in Southern cinema just because their father/ family was successful in the industry! Puneeth was not a product of nepotism; his current fanbase was hard earned, thanks to his acting, dancing abilities, non-conformation to pointless punch dialogues… the list goes on. He had carved an image for himself in Sandalwood. Interestingly, whilst all the above facts about his professional life are true, nobody who was asked to speak about Puneeth, following his death, talks of his career! All that they could reminisce and share about him is his unassuming personality, ever-friendly nature, his philanthropy, his smile🥲, his impeccable professional conduct and his pure soul. Isn’t that what success and life’s victory ultimately is? (He (Puneeth Kumar) sponsored the education of students from more than 45 schools) *Just one of his many philanthropic activities* On a personal front, I’ve myself watched only one of his movies, Raajakumara (2017) which has the famous song Bombe Helutaithe. This movie became the highest grossing Kannada movie ever at that point, beating Mungaru MaLe (2006). But I’ve heard/ watched most of his songs; eagerly waited for and watched his Kannadada Kotyadhipathi, the Kannada adaptation of Kaun Banega Crorepati?; seen his interviews on YouTube and ardently followed him on social media. Most importantly, I do not know how to feel about this! On Wednesday (27th October, 2021), I felt like singing Neenade na, which is a super-hit song from Puneeth sir’s recent Yuvarathnaa movie, sung by Armaan Malik and Shreya Ghoshal. Usually I just hum/ sing and let it go. I don’t know what had gotten on me the other day, I also recorded as I sang! It could’ve been some other song (I love old Kannada classics too), from some other movie! But no, it was a Puneeth song! This makes me feel devastated even more. I feel a strange unexplainable connect, now. I have collected few photos from the internet, attached them to the aforementioned audio clip, made a video and uploaded it on YouTube. Whilst I’m not a trained singer, I consider this surprisingly coincidental recording as my humblest of tributes to the person who’s loved by ~6 crore Kannadigas (yes, he had no haters) and lakhs of other Indians! So this is what shocked me today! I was in shock, still in shock…(probably in the ‘stage of denial’ of grief, as explained by American psychiatrist Elizabeth Kübler!) Mathe hutti banni, Puneeth sir!❤️💔 Signing off by dedicating two lines from his own song Bombe Helutaite from the movie Raajakumara! Ninnanu padedha naavu puneetha! BaaLu nagu nagutha!! We are the lucky ones to have (have had)you! Live happily always!! (in your afterlife😇)

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What made you happy today?
Answer: Making a correct diagnosis! Yesterday, one of my relatives had called me. She complained of ‘feeling too cold even in normal room temperature, when others around don’t feel so’. This is what is known as ‘cold intolerance’ in medical terms. At the same time, it could also be ‘chills’, which is a symptom of conditions like Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) or Malaria. But most of the times, it is associated with fever. In this case though, there was neither fever nor any UTI complaints (increased frequency, burning sensation during urination or lower abdominal pain). So I landed up with a provisional diagnosis of hypothyroidism, of which cold tolerance is a classical symptom. Moreover, hypothyroidism is several times more common in ladies than men. Hence I asked her to get a Thyroid Function Test (TFT) done. The test results came out today. As expected, her TSH level was above normal limits! This is a finding consistent with hypothyroidism. Not surprisingly, her T3 and T4 levels were normal, indicating her to be a case of what we call ‘subclinical hypothyroidism’. Well, that’s what made me happy today - being able to pick symptoms and make a provisional clinical diagnosis even before a lab test would confirm the same. Of course, this is not an out-of-the-world, rare case that needs extra intelligence to pick up. But as a freshly graduated doctor, making such correct diagnoses gives me immense happiness and motivation to keep going. Happy doctors’ day to all fellow doctors!🌸

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: What is something you're not proud of but you continue to do?
Answer: Being a night owl! It is 1.30 AM now, as I write this answer. I’m not one bit proud of staying awake late in the night. I know it is all the same technically, either reading late in the night or rising early and utilising the whole day. But the problem with being a night person is, I am finding it very difficult to get up before 9 AM. This is the time my mother leaves to work. I say bye to her, lock the main door, and again sleep till 10 o’ clock. Thus the start of the day itself feels very lazy. By the time I shower and finish my breakfast it is easily 11 o’ clock, which is quite a late start to a day, right?! Hardly two hours and it is lunch time. I do not postpone my lunch break beyond 1.30 pm due to personal reasons. This short interval of just 2.5 hours between two major meals of the day isn’t very healthy, medically speaking. There are other reasons not to be proud of being a night owl. I miss out on the early morning sunrise, Suprabhata/ Vishnu Sahasranama, potential walk/ jog on the beach road and of course having the breakfast as soon as it’s made! I’m also not being that idealistic guy from an idealistic family having shower early in the morning! Overall, I feel I lose a lot of productive time. These days, it has become a vicious cycle: I get up late, consequently I’m not drained of my energy even after 10 PM, I stay awake (mostly preparing for my PG entrance exams) usually till 2.30 AM or sometimes 3 AM and the cycle continues. One advantage though is, I never get the kind of a silence I get at night during the daytime. There are absolutely no distracting voices or noises - a perfect environment to read/ revise/ focus on anything I am at. That said, I am still not convinced with this whole night owl scene, and yearn to be an early bird with a proper sleep cycle. I tried changing my sleep pattern a couple of times, but failed! I hope I do so before it’s too late.

Question: Would the movie "Poove Unakkaga" be the super-hit that it was if Vijay had agreed to marry the heroine in the climax?

Having said that, the entire movie is about how the hero would go to any extent to make sure the love of his life would unite with her lover against all odds! Vijay’s disappointment, agony and helplessness are beautifully captured, especially when he goes “Andha ponnu lucky dhan ga; naa dhan unlucky! illana na love pannadhe andha ponnuku theriyama irukuma?!” (She’s a indeed a lucky girl! It is I, who am unlucky, for she doesn’t even know I was in love with her!). 27 years after its release, we still speak of the movie and this climax scene in the fag end of 2023, only because he chose not to move on! Had he married the Sangita character who never knew what she wanted and was okay with any decision taken by her family, chances are that Poove Unakkaga would have flopped and be long-forgotten by now! Whilst the climax, or probably the story itself, might be deplorable/ cringeworthy today, it’s totally understandable why it was a crowd-puller back in 1996! Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: If you are much more interested in the pathogenesis and diagnosis of medical conditions than treatment and patient care, does it make you a bad doctor?
Answer: Not at all! I can see myself in this question. I'm a person who loves the pathogenesis (the mechanisms through which a disease evolves) more, than actually knowing about the various treatment options available and cramming them up. (I'm a UG medical student still, nearing Finals). For the same reason, I enjoy reading Robbins more than Harrison. We have been students of Science since years and continue to be; even before we were students of Medicine, we were students of Science! That said, Science can explain anything on Earth and where it fails to, progress has to be made. As far as Medicine is concerned, from the most common symptoms like fever to complex complications, all major diseases (causing significant morbidity and mortality) have scientific basis as to what happens at the cellular (sometimes, even molecular!) level. I feel, in the pursuit of learning to 'just treat' more and more cases and clear off the long queues in OPDs (for which we are trained, at least as UGs), one shouldn't forget the fact that, it is still the Biology that guides all this treatment and its efficacy. Failure to give importance to pathogenesis of diseases, and underestimating the role of research in molecular biology, are what have led to the various lacunae that we have today in treating advanced and rare diseases. End of the day, it's all team work. Surgeries (at least major ones) don't happen without pathologists' or radio-diagnosists' reports or opinion. Microbiologists, whose role is often undermined in recent times, 'diagnose' (of course in lab) deadly infections and issue the most needed 'Drug sensitivity reports', which act like a life-safer many a time, considering the highly resistant bacterial strains and increasing ICU admissions. They are people who love 'diagnosing' more than treatment; they are doctors after all! And the role of Biochemistry in 'diagnosing' Medical conditions is indispensable, without which there is no 'treatment'! The simplest example, I can think of in this regard is the 'treatment' of Diabetes Mellitus. Knowing that blood glucose is increased in Diabetes Mellitus through biochemical tests, and the knowledge through evidence that Insulin reduces the level of blood glucose is what led to the use of various forms of Insulin in therapeutics today! We have come a long way from bovine insulin to recombinant DNA insulin. Thanks to researchers who work on pathogenesis and diagnostics! Going one step ahead, studying for years together the molecular mechanisms of Glucose metabolism and the various receptors involved, today we have an array of drugs known as 'Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs' which have come out to be the saviours of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients. And the increase in life expectancy of these patients, before and after Metformin, I needn't comment I believe! Ultimately it is like 'Any doctor can treat a disease, but only a doctor passionate about the science (pathogenesis) behind, and knows what to look for in different reports (diagnosis), and of course, appreciate with understanding, the signs and symptoms, treats the patient!'. Also, only such doctors are the hope of the future. (We still have deadly diseases that have no treatment or vaccines). This is my humble opinion. Regards, Balakrishnan R.
